claims.text: Mysuru is famous in the world for its sandalwood and rosewood artifacts, stone sculptures, incense sticks, ivory inlay work and silk sarees.

quotes.quote: While marble and granite are used, the main material used for sculpting is the steatite stone. A metamorphic rock, steatite is soft and can be easily carved.

The handiwork belongs to Arun Yogiraj and his team belonging to B Basavanna Shilpi and Sons, now called Kashyapa Shilpa Kala Nikethana. An art and sculpting centre located on the busy Chamaraja Road, this is one place you do not want to miss during your trip to Mysuru.

lede.text: Mysuru is famous in the world for its sandalwood and rosewood artifacts, stone sculptures, incense sticks, ivory inlay work and silk sarees.
Arun Yogiraj, of a family of sculptors, and his team belong to Kashyapa Shilpa Kala Nikethana, an art and sculpting centre on Chamaraja Road in Mysuru.

His 51-inch Ram Lalla idol in black stone was selected for the sanctum sanctorum of the Ayodhya temple, and Mysuru sculptor Paramesh Acharya and his sons crafted a Ganesha idol from Krishna Shile, black stone.
Arun Yogiraj's website describes the Mysore sculpting style he mastered as an improvisation of the methods used in Hoysala architecture.

sentences.text: Mysuru was ruled by the Gangas, Chalukyas, Cholas and Hoysalas before the Vijayanagara kings, and a Hoysala inscription in Mysuru dates back to the 11th and 12th century.

The Keshava Temple at Somanathapura, in the Tirumakudlu Narsipur taluk of Mysore district, is one of the three Hoysala-style temple complexes of the Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas, built between the 12th and 13th centuries.
Sources differ on its year: Citizen Matters and Deccan Herald say Somanatha built it in 1268 under the Hoysala king Narasimha III, while Rice's gazetteers say it was completed in 1269 or in 1270.
Hoysala sculptors signed their work, an unusual practice in the Indian subcontinent, and at Somanathapura the names of Mallithamma, Balayya and Bhamayya are engraved on the walls beside their work.
Rice's gazetteer of the Mysore State says the Silpi, a section of the Badagi or carpenters, are properly sculptors and might be classed among masons.
The Mysore Gazetteer edited by C. Hayavadana Rao says the erection of the New Palace at Mysore afforded an opportunity of reviving local artistic skill.
B. Basavanna Shilpi trained under Shilpi Siddanthi Siddalinga Swami, the Royal Guru of the Mysore Palace, and supplied 64 idols in just 11 months to the Gayatri Temple within the palace premises.
Maharaja Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar presented him with a golden chisel and a silver hammer, and his grandson Arun Yogiraj took up sculpting full-time in 2008.
Arun Yogiraj says selection of stone is key, as the initial slab should be free of cavities and damage of any sort.
Arun Yogiraj says his team's process is handmade: they sketch a rough drawing of the figure directly on the block and start shaping, etching, sculpting and chiselling.

Star of Mysore, describing a sculptors' camp in Mysuru, writes that persistent knocking, proper application of pressure, accurate chiselling and cutting of edges are vital in getting the stone to shape.

Deccan Herald reports that after the final polish Arun Yogiraj's team uses filing tools, sandpaper and natural materials such as coconut oil and dry coconut ash, which render the statue jet black, while his wife is quoted naming coconut and burnt cocoa powder.
Arun Yogiraj told Star of Mysore that Shilpashastra prescribes a silver hammer and golden chisel for the eyes and a fixed muhurta for Nethramilana, the carving of eyes.
He said the beejakshara mantra is first inscribed on the uncarved blank eyes before the eyes are sculpted.
Outlook Traveller reports that a sculpture takes Arun Yogiraj anywhere between two weeks and a month, depending on its size, and Paramesh Acharya's team completed its intricate idol within a month.
Arun Yogiraj's website says he began with Shilpa Shastra, whose precise measurements are often called Thadam in their practice.

The Mysore Gazetteer edited by C. Hayavadana Rao says that, for sculpture, potstone or soapstone is the common material used, and that images of the Gods and ornamental articles are also made from it.

Sources differ on the main stone of Arun Yogiraj's team: Deccan Herald names steatite, a soft metamorphic rock, while Outlook Traveller says he relies equally on marble and granite and sometimes uses softer stones.
Steatite is described as non-reactive, non-porous and non-absorbent, and hence ideal for temple idols worshipped with milk and ghee.
The bust of Nalwadi is of black schist, Krishna Shile, from H. D. Kote, and the black Krishna Shila stone for the Ram Lalla idol was extracted in Gujjegowdanapura in the Mysuru district.

Sculptor Suryaprakash says Krishna Shile is found in the HD Kote area and is traditionally called Balpa stone, and geologist C. Srikantappa describes it as a sky-blue-coloured metamorphic rock of the type called soapstone.

Sources name the stone of the Keshava Temple at Somanathapura differently: UNESCO says chloritic schist, Citizen Matters says soap stone, and Rice's gazetteer says its epic incidents are carved in potstone.

Sahapedia says chlorite schist aids minute ornamentation, as it is softer while carving and gets hardened with exposure, and Deccan Herald says it is softer than the granite and sandstone used earlier.
Arun Yogiraj sculpts in the Dravidian and Hoysala styles, and in a contemporary style as well.
On the Balak Ram idol he carved the jewellery in Hoysala style, the attire in North Indian style and the kankana in South Indian style.
He uses the photographs and drawings his grandfather documented in the early 1970s as references, and calls the craft a fine balance of arithmetic, geometry and art.
His team carved the monolithic statue of Maharaja Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar at Harding Circle, which sources give as 15 feet or 14.5 ft tall.
The Hoysala style combines a multi-tiered frieze, a thematically arranged gallery of religious and epic stories, and stone carvings covering the entire exterior surface.
On the outer wall of the Somanathapura temple, rows of elephants sit below rows of horses and gods and goddesses, and its sculptures show details such as finger rings, bracelets and fingernails.
Star of Mysore reports that after Arun Yogiraj's Balak Ram idol was consecrated at Ayodhya, the work of Mysuru's sculptors gained increasing recognition and demand.
Deccan Herald reported that the availability of raw material depended on the people holding mine licences and permits, and Arun Yogiraj wished artisans could get stone from a government depot.
Deccan Herald reported that Arun Yogiraj runs the Brahmarshi Kashayapa Shilpakala Shala trust, where children are trained in clay modelling, stone balancing and drawing.
As several youngsters inspired by him were inclined to take up Sampradayika Shilpa Kale, he set out to launch a Shilpa Kala Shaala in Mysuru district to train students.

The district of Mysuru is an undulating tableland partly covered by granite outcrops, and Rice's gazetteer says common granite for masonry is abundant throughout the District, where potstone is also found.
Rice's gazetteer of the Mysore State records steatite in the talcose schists in the west of the State, and potstone in beds of considerable size and veins.
Geologist C. Srikantappa told Star of Mysore that high-grade metamorphism altered original minerals of rocks around Mysuru to talc and chlorite, rendering the rock soft and giving the term soapstone.
